title: The Biggest Mistake in Vocabulary Instruction
author: Edulore
summary: Edulore identifies the most common vocabulary instruction mistake—asking 'Does anyone know what this word means?'—and explains why it backfires: students are exposed to inaccurate guesses and competing definitions before anyone has been given the correct information. Effective vocabulary instruction begins with the expert in the room providing the meaning. Drawing on Beck, McKeown, and Kucan's research and a routine adapted from Sean Morrisey and Anita Archer's work, the article walks through a 7-step explicit vocabulary routine: pronounce the word, provide a concise student-friendly definition, give examples and non-examples in context, give structured opportunities to use the word, teach the antonym, check for understanding, and review through spaced retrieval. The goal is turning vocabulary from a passing encounter into durable knowledge through deliberate, repeated exposure—not waiting for incidental acquisition, which consistently widens the existing gap between students with strong and weak vocabulary foundations.
points: Asking students to define an unfamiliar word exposes them to inaccurate guesses and competing ideas before anyone has been given the correct information—the opposite of effective instruction.

Vocabulary knowledge is fundamental to reading comprehension, and incidental acquisition through reading alone consistently reinforces existing gaps between students with strong and weak vocabularies.
Explicit vocabulary routine: pronounce → define → examples/non-examples in context → structured practice → antonym → check for understanding → spaced retrieval.
Teaching antonyms strengthens word knowledge because students learn where a word sits within a network of related meanings, not just what one definition says.
A word appearing in a text does not guarantee students will learn it—they need deliberate instruction with multiple opportunities to hear, say, define, connect, use, and retrieve the word.
quotes: Vocabulary instruction should not begin with students trying to discover the meaning. It should begin with the teacher explicitly teaching the meaning.
Our role is not to find out who already knows the word. Our role is to ensure every student learns it.
Students who enter school with a larger vocabulary tend to acquire new words more easily, while students with smaller vocabularies often experience a widening gap over time.
Knowing a definition is not the same as being able to use a word. Students need to practise.

Words become clearer when students understand what they are and what they are not. Teaching antonyms strengthens students' understanding because they are learning where a word sits within a network of related meanings.
A word appearing in a text does not guarantee students will learn it. Students need deliberate instruction.
